title: Algebra 1
description: High school Algebra 1: real numbers, linear equations and inequalities, absolute value, functions and lines, systems, exponents, polynomials and factoring, quadratics, square roots, exponential growth and decay, sequences, and data analysis. Every lesson teaches with worked examples and graphs, and every skill has generated practice problems.

lessons.title: Real numbers and their properties
lessons.body:
Algebra is arithmetic with the numbers left unspecified. Before we start replacing numbers with letters, it pays to be precise about which numbers we mean and which rules they obey, because every algebra step you will ever take is one of these rules applied to a letter instead of a digit. This lesson sorts the numbers into families, puts them on the number line, defines absolute value, and names the properties that make algebra work.

## The families of numbers

The numbers you count with, $1, 2, 3, \dots$, are the **[[natural numbers]]**. Add $0$ and you get the **[[whole numbers]]**. Add the negatives, $\dots, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots$, and you have the **[[integers]]**.

A **[[rational number]]** is any number you can write as a fraction $\dfrac{p}{q}$ of two integers with $q \ne 0$. Every integer is rational ($7 = \tfrac71$), and so are $-\tfrac{3}{4}$, $0.25 = \tfrac14$ and $0.\overline{3} = \tfrac13$. In decimal form, a rational number either stops (terminates) or repeats a block of digits forever. That happens because long division by $q$ can only leave the remainders $0, 1, \dots, q-1$; once a remainder comes back, the digits cycle.

An **[[irrational number]]** is a real number that cannot be written as a fraction of integers. Its decimal goes on forever without repeating. The standard examples are $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41421$, $\sqrt{5}$, and $\pi \approx 3.14159$. The square root of any whole number that is not a perfect square is irrational.

Together, the rational and irrational numbers make up the **[[real numbers]]**, written $\mathbb{R}$. Every real number is exactly one of rational or irrational, and the sets nest like this:

| Set | Examples | Contains |
|---|---|---|
| Natural numbers | $1, 2, 3$ | — |
| Whole numbers | $0, 1, 2$ | naturals |
| Integers | $-5, 0, 12$ | wholes |
| Rational numbers | $-\tfrac{2}{3}, 0.75, 4$ | integers |
| Irrational numbers | $\sqrt{3}, \pi$ | (no overlap with rationals) |
| Real numbers | all of the above | rationals and irrationals |

### Example 1

Classify $-6$, $\tfrac{9}{3}$, $0.\overline{18}$, $\sqrt{49}$ and $\sqrt{50}$.

- $-6$ is an integer, so it is also rational and real (not whole, because it is negative).
- $\tfrac{9}{3}$ looks like a fraction, but it simplifies to $3$: a natural number, and therefore also whole, integer, rational and real. Always simplify before classifying.
- $0.\overline{18}$ repeats, so it is rational. (It equals $\tfrac{18}{99} = \tfrac{2}{11}$.)
- $\sqrt{49} = 7$ is natural.
- $\sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}$ is irrational, because 50 is not a perfect square.

## The number line and order

Every real number has a spot on the **[[number line]]**: zero in the middle, positives to the right, negatives to the left. A number is greater than another exactly when it sits farther to the right. That is why $-2 > -5$ even though 5 is "bigger": $-2$ is to the right of $-5$.

```numberline
{"x": [-6, 6], "points": [{"at": [-5, 0], "label": "-5"}, {"at": [-2, 0], "label": "-2"}, {"at": [1.5, 0], "label": "1.5"}, {"at": [3.14159, 0], "label": "π"}], "caption": "Numbers further right are greater: -5 < -2 < 1.5 < π"}
```

The symbols $<$, $\le$, $>$ and $\ge$ compare numbers. The point of the symbol always faces the smaller number.

## Absolute value

The **[[absolute value]]** of a number, written $|a|$, is its distance from zero on the number line. Distances are never negative, so $|5| = 5$, $|-5| = 5$ and $|0| = 0$. As a formula,

$$|a| = \begin{cases} a & \text{if } a \ge 0 \\ -a & \text{if } a < 0 \end{cases}$$

The second line confuses people: if $a$ is negative, then $-a$ is positive. For $a = -5$, $-a = -(-5) = 5$.

Because absolute value measures distance from zero, $|a - b|$ measures the distance between $a$ and $b$. The distance from $-3$ to $4$ is $|4 - (-3)| = |7| = 7$; you can count the seven steps on the number line. Order doesn't matter: $|-3 - 4| = |-7| = 7$ too.

## Operations with signed numbers and fractions

The sign rules follow from the number line. Adding a negative moves left; subtracting a number is the same as adding its **[[opposite]]** (so $5 - (-2) = 5 + 2 = 7$). For multiplication and division, two like signs give a positive result and unlike signs give a negative one.

Fractions add only over a common denominator, because you can only add pieces of the same size:

$$\frac{a}{b} + \frac{c}{d} = \frac{ad + bc}{bd}, \qquad \frac{a}{b} \cdot \frac{c}{d} = \frac{ac}{bd}, \qquad \frac{a}{b} \div \frac{c}{d} = \frac{a}{b} \cdot \frac{d}{c}.$$

Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its **[[reciprocal]]**, the fraction flipped upside down. The reciprocal of $\tfrac{c}{d}$ is $\tfrac{d}{c}$, and a number times its reciprocal is 1.

### Example 2

Compute $\dfrac{5}{6} - \dfrac{3}{4}$ and $-\dfrac{2}{3} \div \dfrac{8}{9}$.

1. The least common denominator of 6 and 4 is 12. Rewrite: $\tfrac{10}{12} - \tfrac{9}{12} = \tfrac{1}{12}$.
2. Division becomes multiplication by the reciprocal: $-\tfrac{2}{3} \cdot \tfrac{9}{8} = -\tfrac{18}{24}$.
3. Reduce by the common factor 6: $-\tfrac{3}{4}$. The sign is negative because the signs were unlike.

## The properties of real numbers

These are the rules that every algebraic manipulation rests on. They hold for all real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$.

| Property | Addition | Multiplication |
|---|---|---|
| **[[Commutative property]]** | $a + b = b + a$ | $ab = ba$ |
| **[[Associative property]]** | $(a + b) + c = a + (b + c)$ | $(ab)c = a(bc)$ |
| **[[Identity property]]** | $a + 0 = a$ | $a \cdot 1 = a$ |
| **[[Inverse property]]** | $a + (-a) = 0$ | $a \cdot \tfrac{1}{a} = 1$ for $a \ne 0$ |

and the one that links the two operations, the **[[distributive property]]**:

$$a(b + c) = ab + ac.$$

Commutative means order can change; associative means grouping can change. Zero is the **[[additive identity]]** and 1 is the **[[multiplicative identity]]**, because adding 0 or multiplying by 1 leaves a number unchanged. The **[[additive inverse]]** of $a$ is $-a$ and the **[[multiplicative inverse]]** of $a$ is its reciprocal $\tfrac1a$.

Why does the distributive property hold? Picture a rectangle $a$ units tall and $b + c$ units wide. Its area is $a(b + c)$, but you can also split it into an $a \times b$ piece and an $a \times c$ piece, with total area $ab + ac$. Same rectangle, same area.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [5, 0], [5, 2], [0, 2]]}], "segments": [{"from": [3, 0], "to": [3, 2], "dashed": true}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [3, 0], "label": "b"}, {"from": [3, 0], "to": [5, 0], "label": "c"}, {"from": [0, 2], "to": [0, 0], "label": "a"}], "labels": [{"at": [1.5, 1], "text": "ab"}, {"at": [4, 1], "text": "ac"}], "caption": "a(b + c) = ab + ac: one rectangle, two pieces"}
```

Subtraction and division are not commutative or associative: $5 - 3 \ne 3 - 5$ and $(12 \div 6) \div 2 = 1$ while $12 \div (6 \div 2) = 4$. That is one reason we often rewrite subtraction as adding the opposite.

Finally, division by zero is **[[undefined]]**. If $\tfrac{6}{0}$ were some number $n$, then $n \cdot 0$ would have to equal 6, but anything times 0 is 0. (By contrast $\tfrac{0}{6} = 0$ is perfectly fine.)

### Example 3

Name the property used in each step of $3(x + 4) + 2x = 3x + 12 + 2x = 3x + 2x + 12 = 5x + 12$.

1. $3(x + 4) = 3x + 12$: the distributive property.
2. $12 + 2x = 2x + 12$: the commutative property of addition, to bring like terms together.
3. $3x + 2x = (3 + 2)x = 5x$: the distributive property again, used in reverse.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking a fraction is automatically "not an integer." $\tfrac{12}{4}$ is the integer 3.
- Calling every square root irrational. $\sqrt{16} = 4$ is rational; only roots of non-perfect squares are irrational.
- Writing $|-a| = a$ for every $a$. If $a$ is already negative, say $a = -3$, then $|-a| = |3| = 3 = -a$.
- Adding fractions straight across: $\tfrac12 + \tfrac13 \ne \tfrac25$.
- Distributing to only the first term: $4(x + 3) = 4x + 12$, not $4x + 3$.

## Key points

- Naturals ⊂ wholes ⊂ integers ⊂ rationals ⊂ reals; irrationals are the reals that are not rational.
- Rational decimals terminate or repeat; irrational decimals do neither.
- $|a|$ is distance from 0, and $|a - b|$ is the distance between $a$ and $b$.
- Commutative (order), associative (grouping), identity (0 and 1), inverse (opposite and reciprocal), and distributive properties justify every algebra step.
- Division by zero is undefined.

lessons.title: Expressions, order of operations, and like terms
lessons.body:
With the real numbers and their properties in hand, we can start writing algebra. This lesson covers the vocabulary of expressions, the agreed order for carrying out operations, how to evaluate an expression for given values, and how to simplify by combining like terms. These are the moves you will make inside every equation that follows.

## Variables, terms and expressions

A **[[variable]]** is a letter that stands for a number we either don't know yet or want to leave open, such as $x$ in $3x + 5$. A fixed number like 5 is a **[[constant]]**. An **[[algebraic expression]]** combines variables and constants with operations: $3x + 5$, $\tfrac{a + b}{2}$, $4x^2 - 7xy$.

The pieces of an expression that are added together are its **[[terms]]**. In $4x^2 - 7xy + 9$ the terms are $4x^2$, $-7xy$ and $9$. Notice the minus sign travels with the term that follows it: subtracting $7xy$ is the same as adding $-7xy$. The number in front of a variable part is its **[[coefficient]]**: here 4 and $-7$. A term with no variable, like 9, is a **[[constant term]]**.

An expression is not an equation. An expression has no equals sign; you can simplify or evaluate it, but you can't "solve" it.

## Order of operations

The expression $2 + 3 \cdot 4$ would give 20 if you worked left to right and 14 if you multiplied first. Mathematicians agreed long ago to the **[[order of operations]]**, so everyone gets 14:

1. Grouping first: parentheses, brackets, fraction bars, absolute value bars and radicals all group. Work from the innermost group outward.
2. Exponents next.
3. Multiplication and division, from left to right, as they appear.
4. Addition and subtraction, from left to right, as they appear.

The memory aid **[[PEMDAS]]** (Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication/Division, Addition/Subtraction) is handy, but it hides a trap: multiplication does not come before division, and addition does not come before subtraction. Each pair has equal rank and is done left to right. So $12 \div 3 \cdot 2 = 4 \cdot 2 = 8$, not $12 \div 6 = 2$.

A second trap is the exponent on a negative number. An exponent applies only to what is immediately to its left. In $-3^2$ the exponent applies to 3, and the negative sign is applied after: $-3^2 = -(3^2) = -9$. To square $-3$ you must write $(-3)^2 = 9$.

### Example 1

Evaluate $18 - 2\left[5 - (1 - 4)^2\right] \div 4$.

1. Innermost group: $1 - 4 = -3$.
2. Exponent: $(-3)^2 = 9$.
3. Finish the bracket: $5 - 9 = -4$.
4. Now $18 - 2(-4) \div 4$. Multiplication and division left to right: $2(-4) = -8$, then $-8 \div 4 = -2$.
5. Finally $18 - (-2) = 20$.

A fraction bar groups everything above it and everything below it. In $\dfrac{6 + 10}{2 \cdot 4}$, finish the numerator (16) and the denominator (8) before dividing: the value is 2.

## Evaluating expressions

To **[[evaluate]]** an expression, substitute the given value for each variable and then follow the order of operations. Always substitute in parentheses, especially for negative numbers: it keeps the signs and exponents straight.

### Example 2

Evaluate $2x^2 - 3xy + y$ when $x = -2$ and $y = 5$.

1. Substitute with parentheses: $2(-2)^2 - 3(-2)(5) + (5)$.
2. Exponent first: $(-2)^2 = 4$, so the first term is $2 \cdot 4 = 8$.
3. Second term: $-3(-2)(5) = 30$. Two negatives make a positive.
4. Add: $8 + 30 + 5 = 43$.

Without the parentheses, someone might write $2 \cdot -2^2$ and get $-8$ for the first term, which is the exponent trap again.

## Like terms and simplifying

**[[Like terms]]** have exactly the same variable part: the same letters raised to the same powers. $5x^2$ and $-2x^2$ are like terms; $5x^2$ and $5x$ are not, and neither are $3xy$ and $3x$. Constants are like terms with each other.

You combine like terms by adding their coefficients. This is just the distributive property used in reverse:

$$5x^2 - 2x^2 = (5 - 2)x^2 = 3x^2.$$

Unlike terms cannot be combined: $3x + 4y$ is already as simple as it gets, much as 3 apples plus 4 oranges can't be called 7 of anything.

To **[[simplify]]** an expression, first remove parentheses with the distributive property, then combine like terms. Pay attention to a minus sign in front of parentheses. It means "multiply by $-1$," so it changes the sign of every term inside:

$$-(2x - 7) = -2x + 7.$$

### Example 3

Simplify $4(2x - 3) - (5x - 8) + x^2$.

1. Distribute the 4: $8x - 12$.
2. Distribute the $-1$: $-5x + 8$.
3. The expression is now $8x - 12 - 5x + 8 + x^2$.
4. Combine like terms: $x$-terms $8x - 5x = 3x$; constants $-12 + 8 = -4$; the $x^2$ term has no partner.
5. Result, written with the highest power first: $x^2 + 3x - 4$.

### Example 4

Simplify $3a - 2(4a + b) + 6b$.

1. Distribute $-2$ to both terms: $-8a - 2b$.
2. Now $3a - 8a - 2b + 6b$.
3. Combine: $-5a + 4b$.

A common slip is distributing only $2$ and writing $-8a + 2b$; the negative belongs to the multiplier and must hit both terms.

## Translating words into expressions

Algebra lets you describe a quantity before you know its value. Some standard translations:

| Words | Expression |
|---|---|
| 7 more than a number | $n + 7$ |
| 7 less than a number | $n - 7$ (not $7 - n$) |
| twice a number, decreased by 3 | $2n - 3$ |
| the quotient of a number and 4 | $\tfrac{n}{4}$ |
| the square of the sum of $a$ and $b$ | $(a + b)^2$ |
| the sum of the squares of $a$ and $b$ | $a^2 + b^2$ |

"Less than" reverses the order you read it in: "5 less than $x$" starts at $x$ and takes 5 away.

## Common mistakes

- Doing multiplication before division (or addition before subtraction) regardless of position. Pairs of equal rank go left to right.
- Treating $-x^2$ as $(-x)^2$. When $x = 3$, $-x^2 = -9$.
- Forgetting to distribute a negative sign to every term in parentheses.
- Combining unlike terms, like $2x + 3x^2 = 5x^3$. The powers differ, so these don't combine.
- Substituting negative values without parentheses.

## Key points

- Terms are the parts being added; a coefficient is the number multiplying a term's variable part.
- Order of operations: grouping, exponents, multiplication and division (left to right), addition and subtraction (left to right).
- An exponent applies only to what is directly before it: $-3^2 = -9$ but $(-3)^2 = 9$.
- To evaluate, substitute in parentheses, then follow the order of operations.
- Like terms share the same variables and powers; combine them by adding coefficients (the distributive property in reverse).

lessons.title: Solving linear equations
lessons.body:
Now that you can simplify expressions, you can solve equations. An equation says two expressions are equal; solving it means finding every value of the variable that makes that statement true. This lesson handles **[[linear equations]]**, the ones where the variable appears only to the first power, like $3x - 7 = 11$ or $2(x + 1) = 5x - 4$. Everything later in algebra builds on doing this quickly and reliably.

## What it means to solve

A **[[solution]]** of an equation is a value of the variable that makes it true. $x = 6$ is a solution of $3x - 7 = 11$ because $3(6) - 7 = 11$. The set of all solutions is the **[[solution set]]**.

Two equations are **[[equivalent equations]]** when they have the same solution set. Solving is a chain of equivalent equations, each simpler than the last, until the variable stands alone: $x = \text{number}$.

## The properties of equality

What moves keep an equation equivalent? Think of a balance scale: whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other.

- **[[Addition property of equality]]**: if $a = b$, then $a + c = b + c$ (and likewise $a - c = b - c$).
- **[[Multiplication property of equality]]**: if $a = b$, then $ac = bc$, and $\tfrac{a}{c} = \tfrac{b}{c}$ for $c \ne 0$.

The restriction $c \ne 0$ matters. Multiplying both sides by 0 turns any equation into $0 = 0$ and destroys the information, and dividing by 0 is undefined.

Each property undoes an operation. Addition undoes subtraction, division undoes multiplication. To isolate the variable, undo the operations in the reverse order from how they were applied to it, the way you'd take off shoes before socks.

### Example 1

Solve $3x - 7 = 11$.

The expression $3x - 7$ was built by multiplying $x$ by 3 and then subtracting 7. Undo in reverse order.

1. Undo the subtraction: add 7 to both sides. $3x = 18$.
2. Undo the multiplication: divide both sides by 3. $x = 6$.
3. Check: $3(6) - 7 = 18 - 7 = 11$. True.

## A general strategy

Most linear equations fall to the same five steps:

1. Clear fractions or decimals if you like, by multiplying both sides by a common denominator or a power of 10.
2. Simplify each side: distribute, then combine like terms.
3. Collect variable terms on one side and constants on the other, using the addition property.
4. Isolate the variable using the multiplication property.
5. Check your answer in the original equation.

### Example 2

Solve $2(x + 1) = 5x - 4$.

1. Distribute on the left: $2x + 2 = 5x - 4$.
2. Collect $x$-terms. Subtracting $2x$ from both sides keeps the coefficient positive: $2 = 3x - 4$.
3. Add 4: $6 = 3x$.
4. Divide by 3: $x = 2$.
5. Check: left side $2(3) = 6$; right side $5(2) - 4 = 6$. True.

### Example 3

Solve $\dfrac{x}{4} - \dfrac{x - 2}{6} = 1$.

1. The least common denominator of 4 and 6 is 12. Multiply every term on both sides by 12:
$$12 \cdot \frac{x}{4} - 12 \cdot \frac{x - 2}{6} = 12 \cdot 1.$$
2. Simplify: $3x - 2(x - 2) = 12$. Keep the parentheses: the whole numerator $x - 2$ is multiplied by 2.
3. Distribute: $3x - 2x + 4 = 12$, so $x + 4 = 12$.
4. Subtract 4: $x = 8$.
5. Check: $\tfrac84 - \tfrac{6}{6} = 2 - 1 = 1$. True.

Clearing fractions works because of the multiplication property: multiplying both sides by 12 doesn't change the solution set. The same trick handles decimals. For $0.3x + 1.2 = 0.05x + 2.2$, multiply by 100 to get $30x + 120 = 5x + 220$, then $25x = 100$ and $x = 4$.

## Seeing a solution on a graph

You can picture an equation as two graphs, one for each side. For $2(x + 1) = 5x - 4$, graph $y = 2(x + 1)$ and $y = 5x - 4$. The solution is the $x$-coordinate where the two lines cross.

```plot
{"x": [-2, 5], "y": [-6, 12], "functions": [{"f": "2*(x + 1)", "label": "y = 2(x + 1)"}, {"f": "5*x - 4", "label": "y = 5x - 4", "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [2, 6], "label": "(2, 6)"}], "caption": "The two sides are equal where the lines meet, at x = 2"}
```

## Equations with no solution or infinitely many

Usually a linear equation has exactly one solution. Two other outcomes are possible, and you recognize them when the variable disappears.

- If you reach a false statement like $0 = 5$, the equation has **[[no solution]]**. Its solution set is the empty set, written $\varnothing$. Such an equation is a **[[contradiction]]**.
- If you reach a true statement like $0 = 0$ or $7 = 7$, every real number is a solution. Such an equation is an **[[identity]]**.

An equation that is true for some values and false for others, like $3x - 7 = 11$, is a **[[conditional equation]]**.

### Example 4

Solve $4(x - 2) + 3 = 4x - 1$ and $3(2x + 1) = 6x + 3$.

1. First equation: the left side simplifies to $4x - 8 + 3 = 4x - 5$. So $4x - 5 = 4x - 1$. Subtract $4x$: $-5 = -1$, which is false. No solution.
2. Second equation: the left side is $6x + 3$, identical to the right side. Subtract $6x$: $3 = 3$, always true. Every real number is a solution.

On a graph, the first case is two parallel lines that never meet, and the second is the same line drawn twice.

## Common mistakes

- Doing an operation to only one side, or to only one term on a side. When you multiply to clear fractions, every term on both sides gets multiplied.
- Dropping parentheses around a numerator: $-\tfrac{x - 2}{6}$ times 12 is $-2(x - 2) = -2x + 4$, not $-2x - 4$.
- Dividing by the coefficient but losing its sign: from $-4x = 12$, $x = -3$, not $3$.
- Writing "$x = 0$" for an equation like $-5 = -1$. A false statement means no solution at all, not a solution of 0.
- Skipping the check. Substituting back takes seconds and catches most slips.

## Key points

- Solving means producing simpler equivalent equations until the variable is alone.
- You may add, subtract, multiply or divide both sides by the same quantity (never multiply or divide by 0).
- Undo operations in reverse order: usually addition/subtraction first, then multiplication/division.
- Clear fractions by multiplying both sides by the least common denominator.
- If the variable vanishes, a false statement means no solution and a true statement means all real numbers.

lessons.title: Literal equations and formulas
lessons.body:
Formulas are equations with several letters: $d = rt$, $A = \tfrac12 bh$, $F = \tfrac95 C + 32$. Often a formula is written for one variable but you need another. Rearranging it is the same skill as the last lesson, solving a linear equation, except the "numbers" you move around are letters. This lesson shows how to do that cleanly, and when you're allowed to divide by a letter.

## Literal equations

A **[[literal equation]]** is an equation with two or more variables. A **[[formula]]** is a literal equation that expresses a known relationship, such as the perimeter of a rectangle $P = 2l + 2w$.

To **[[solve for]]** a variable means to isolate it, so that it appears alone on one side and nowhere on the other. The other letters are treated exactly as if they were numbers. A good habit: imagine the other letters are specific numbers, decide what you would do, then do the same thing with the letters.

### Example 1

Solve $P = 2l + 2w$ for $w$.

Pretend it said $20 = 2(3) + 2w$. You would subtract the $2l$ term, then divide by 2. Do the same with letters.

1. Subtract $2l$ from both sides: $P - 2l = 2w$.
2. Divide both sides by 2: $w = \dfrac{P - 2l}{2}$.

You may also write the result as $w = \tfrac{P}{2} - l$; both are correct. What you must not write is $w = P - 2l \div 2$, which by order of operations means $P - l$. Use a fraction bar or parentheses to keep $P - 2l$ together.

## Dividing by a variable

When you divide both sides by a letter, you are assuming it isn't zero. In formulas this is usually automatic: a rate, a length or a time can't be zero in a meaningful problem. Still, it's good practice to note it. Solving $d = rt$ for $t$ gives $t = \tfrac{d}{r}$, valid for $r \ne 0$.

### Example 2

Convert the temperature formula $F = \tfrac95 C + 32$ into a formula for $C$.

1. Subtract 32: $F - 32 = \tfrac95 C$.
2. Multiply both sides by the reciprocal $\tfrac59$: $C = \tfrac59(F - 32)$.
3. Check with a known pair: water boils at $F = 212$. $\tfrac59(212 - 32) = \tfrac59(180) = 100$. Correct.

Multiplying by the reciprocal is cleaner than dividing by a fraction, and it's the same operation.

## When the variable appears twice

If the variable you want shows up in more than one term, gather those terms on one side and **[[factor]]** the variable out. That's the distributive property in reverse, and it's the key step people miss.

### Example 3

Solve $ax + b = cx + d$ for $x$.

1. Collect the $x$-terms on the left: $ax - cx = d - b$.
2. Factor out $x$: $x(a - c) = d - b$.
3. Divide by $a - c$ (assuming $a \ne c$): $x = \dfrac{d - b}{a - c}$.

### Example 4

The amount in an account with simple interest is $A = P + Prt$. Solve for $P$.

1. $P$ appears in two terms on the right. Factor it out: $A = P(1 + rt)$.
2. Divide by $1 + rt$: $P = \dfrac{A}{1 + rt}$.

Trying to "subtract $Prt$" first leaves $A - Prt = P$, which still has $P$ on both sides. Not solved.

## Using a formula once it's rearranged

Rearranging first pays off when you'll use a formula many times, or when it makes the arithmetic cleaner.

### Example 5

A trapezoid has area $A = \tfrac12 h(b_1 + b_2)$. If its area is 60 square cm, its height is 8 cm and one base is 6 cm, how long is the other base?

1. Solve for $b_2$. Multiply by 2: $2A = h(b_1 + b_2)$.
2. Divide by $h$: $\tfrac{2A}{h} = b_1 + b_2$.
3. Subtract $b_1$: $b_2 = \dfrac{2A}{h} - b_1$.
4. Substitute: $b_2 = \tfrac{2(60)}{8} - 6 = 15 - 6 = 9$ cm.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [9, 0], [7, 4], [1, 4]]}], "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [9, 0], "label": "b₂ = ?"}, {"from": [1, 4], "to": [7, 4], "label": "b₁ = 6"}, {"from": [6, 0], "to": [6, 4], "dashed": true, "label": "h = 8"}], "caption": "Trapezoid with area 60 (not to scale)"}
```

### Example 6

The surface area of a closed cylinder is $S = 2\pi r h + 2\pi r^2$. Solve for $h$, then find the height of a can with $S = 100\pi$ square cm and $r = 5$ cm.

1. The term without $h$ is $2\pi r^2$. Subtract it: $S - 2\pi r^2 = 2\pi r h$.
2. Divide both sides by $2\pi r$: $h = \dfrac{S - 2\pi r^2}{2\pi r}$.
3. Substitute: $h = \dfrac{100\pi - 2\pi(25)}{2\pi(5)} = \dfrac{50\pi}{10\pi} = 5$ cm.

Notice that $\pi$ cancels. Keeping $\pi$ as a symbol until the end, instead of using 3.14 early, gives an exact answer and less rounding.

## Checking a rearranged formula

Two quick checks catch most errors.

- *Units.* In $t = \tfrac{d}{r}$, miles divided by miles per hour gives hours, which is right for a time. If you had written $t = dr$, the units would be miles squared per hour, which can't be a time.
- *Known values.* Pick numbers that satisfy the original formula, such as $d = 120$, $r = 40$, $t = 3$, and confirm the new formula reproduces the one you solved for.

## A useful table of formulas

| Formula | Meaning | Solved for another variable |
|---|---|---|
| $d = rt$ | distance = rate × time | $r = \tfrac{d}{t}$, $t = \tfrac{d}{r}$ |
| $I = Prt$ | simple interest | $r = \tfrac{I}{Pt}$ |
| $A = lw$ | rectangle area | $w = \tfrac{A}{l}$ |
| $P = 2l + 2w$ | rectangle perimeter | $l = \tfrac{P - 2w}{2}$ |
| $C = 2\pi r$ | circle circumference | $r = \tfrac{C}{2\pi}$ |
| $y = mx + b$ | line | $x = \tfrac{y - b}{m}$, $m = \tfrac{y - b}{x}$ |

## Common mistakes

- Dividing only one term by the coefficient: from $2w = P - 2l$, writing $w = P - l$ instead of $w = \tfrac{P - 2l}{2}$.
- Leaving the target variable on both sides. If it appears twice, collect and factor.
- "Cancelling" across a sum: $\tfrac{P - 2l}{2}$ is not $P - l$, because the 2 must divide both terms.
- Forgetting that dividing by an expression assumes it's not zero.

## Key points

- A literal equation has several variables; solving for one means isolating it on one side.
- Treat the other letters like numbers and use the same moves as for linear equations.
- If the target variable appears in several terms, gather those terms and factor the variable out.
- Use a fraction bar or parentheses so a whole side gets divided.
- Check a rearranged formula with a pair of values you know.

lessons.title: Linear equations in applications
lessons.body:
The point of solving equations is to answer questions about the world. This lesson turns word problems into linear equations, using what you learned about translating words (Lesson 2) and solving (Lessons 3 and 4). The algebra is usually easy; the skill is setting up the equation. A steady routine makes that much easier.

## A routine for word problems

1. Read and identify what is being asked. Write it down in words.
2. Name the unknown with a variable, and write the other unknown quantities in terms of it. "Let $x$ = the width in meters."
3. Write an equation that says the same thing as the problem. Look for the fact that gives two expressions for the same quantity.
4. Solve the equation.
5. Answer the question in words, with units, and check it against the original wording (not against your equation, which might be wrong).

A table or sketch often helps with step 3.

## Number and consecutive integer problems

**[[Consecutive integers]]** follow one another: $n$, $n + 1$, $n + 2$. Consecutive even integers (like 8, 10, 12) and consecutive odd integers (like 7, 9, 11) both step by 2: $n$, $n + 2$, $n + 4$. The step is 2 in both cases; whether they are even or odd depends only on the first one.

### Example 1

The sum of three consecutive odd integers is 141. Find them.

1. Let $n$ be the smallest. The others are $n + 2$ and $n + 4$.
2. Equation: $n + (n + 2) + (n + 4) = 141$.
3. Solve: $3n + 6 = 141$, so $3n = 135$ and $n = 45$.
4. The integers are 45, 47 and 49. Check: they're odd, consecutive, and sum to 141.

## Percent problems

"Percent" means "per hundred," so 8% is $0.08$. The key relationship is

$$\text{part} = \text{rate} \times \text{whole}.$$

For a **[[percent change]]**, compare the change with the original amount:

$$\text{percent change} = \frac{\text{new} - \text{original}}{\text{original}} \times 100\%.$$

A price rising by 20% becomes $1.20$ times the original, and a price falling by 20% becomes $0.80$ times the original. Writing increases and decreases as multipliers like this avoids most errors.

### Example 2

After a 15% discount, a jacket costs $68. What was the original price?

1. Let $p$ be the original price. A 15% discount leaves 85% of it.
2. Equation: $0.85p = 68$.
3. Solve: $p = 68 / 0.85 = 80$.
4. The original price was $80. Check: 15% of 80 is 12, and 80 − 12 = 68.

The tempting mistake is to add 15% of 68 back on, which gives $78.20. The discount was 15% of the original price, not of the sale price.

## Distance, rate and time

Motion at constant speed obeys $d = rt$. A table with one row per moving object keeps things organized.

### Example 3

Two cyclists leave the same point at the same time and ride in opposite directions, one at 14 mph and the other at 18 mph. How long until they are 56 miles apart?

| | Rate | Time | Distance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cyclist A | 14 | $t$ | $14t$ |
| Cyclist B | 18 | $t$ | $18t$ |

1. They move apart, so their distances add up to the gap: $14t + 18t = 56$.
2. Solve: $32t = 56$, so $t = 1.75$ hours.
3. Answer: 1.75 hours, which is 1 hour 45 minutes. Check: $14(1.75) = 24.5$ and $18(1.75) = 31.5$, total 56.

When one object chases another, the equation is instead that the distances are equal at the moment one catches up.

## Geometry problems

Use the formula for the figure and express every dimension using one variable.

### Example 4

A rectangular garden is 3 meters longer than twice its width, and its perimeter is 48 meters. Find its dimensions.

1. Let $w$ be the width. Then the length is $2w + 3$.
2. Perimeter: $2w + 2(2w + 3) = 48$.
3. Solve: $2w + 4w + 6 = 48$, so $6w = 42$ and $w = 7$.
4. Length: $2(7) + 3 = 17$. The garden is 7 m by 17 m. Check: $2(7) + 2(17) = 48$.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [17, 0], [17, 7], [0, 7]]}], "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [17, 0], "label": "2w + 3 = 17"}, {"from": [0, 7], "to": [0, 0], "label": "w = 7"}], "caption": "The garden: width 7 m, length 17 m"}
```

## Value and mixture problems

When items of different values are combined, the total value is the sum of (number of items × value of each). The same idea covers mixing solutions: the amount of pure substance is (volume × concentration).

### Example 5

How many liters of a 40% acid solution must be added to 10 liters of a 15% solution to make a 25% solution?

| | Liters | Concentration | Liters of acid |
|---|---|---|---|
| 15% solution | 10 | 0.15 | 1.5 |
| 40% solution | $x$ | 0.40 | $0.40x$ |
| Mixture | $10 + x$ | 0.25 | $0.25(10 + x)$ |

1. The acid in the mixture is the acid from both parts: $1.5 + 0.40x = 0.25(10 + x)$.
2. Distribute: $1.5 + 0.40x = 2.5 + 0.25x$.
3. Collect: $0.15x = 1$, so $x = \tfrac{1}{0.15} = \tfrac{20}{3} \approx 6.67$ liters.
4. Check: total acid $1.5 + 0.40(6.67) \approx 4.17$ liters in $16.67$ liters, which is 25%.

The mixture's concentration must land between the two ingredients' concentrations (here between 15% and 40%). If your setup gives a target outside that range, something is wrong.

## Linear models of cost

Many costs have a fixed part plus a part that grows at a constant rate per unit: a phone plan with a monthly fee plus a charge per gigabyte, or a taxi with a base fare plus a charge per mile. The total is

$$\text{total} = \text{fixed cost} + \text{rate} \times \text{number of units}.$$

### Example 6

A taxi charges $3.50 plus $2.25 per mile. A ride cost $30.50. How far was it?

1. Let $m$ be the miles. Equation: $3.50 + 2.25m = 30.50$.
2. Subtract 3.50: $2.25m = 27$.
3. Divide: $m = 12$ miles.

This kind of relationship is a linear function, which we'll study properly in Module 3.

## Common mistakes

- Using $n$, $n + 1$, $n + 2$ for consecutive odd or even integers. They step by 2.
- Taking a percent of the wrong base, such as the sale price instead of the original price.
- Adding a percent increase and then subtracting the same percent decrease and expecting to return to the start: a 10% rise and then a 10% fall gives $1.1 \times 0.9 = 0.99$ of the original.
- Mixing units, such as a speed in miles per hour with a time in minutes.
- Answering with the value of the variable when the question asked for something else (the length, not the width; the time in minutes, not hours).

## Key points

- Name the unknown, express the other quantities in terms of it, and find the fact that gives an equation.
- Consecutive integers step by 1; consecutive even or odd integers step by 2.
- Part = rate × whole; percent change compares the change to the original.
- Use $d = rt$ with a table for motion problems.
- Answer the actual question, with units, and check against the original words.

lessons.title: Linear and compound inequalities
lessons.body:
An equation pins a variable to particular values. An inequality allows a whole range: "at least 18 years old," "under 2,000 calories," "between 60 and 75 degrees." Solving linear inequalities uses almost exactly the steps from Lesson 3, with one important new rule. This lesson also introduces interval notation for writing the answers, and compound inequalities that join two conditions with "and" or "or."

## Inequalities and their solutions

A **[[linear inequality]]** looks like a linear equation with $=$ replaced by $<$, $\le$, $>$ or $\ge$, for example $2x - 5 < 7$. A solution is any number that makes it true, and there are usually infinitely many. For $2x - 5 < 7$, the number 3 works ($1 < 7$) and so does $-100$, but 6 doesn't ($7 < 7$ is false).

## Solving: the one new rule

Adding or subtracting the same number on both sides keeps an inequality true: if $a < b$, then $a + c < b + c$. Shifting both numbers along the number line keeps their order.

Multiplying or dividing by a positive number also keeps the order. But multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses it. Take the true statement $2 < 5$ and multiply both sides by $-1$: you get $-2$ and $-5$, and on the number line $-2$ is to the right, so $-2 > -5$. Multiplying by a negative reflects the number line across 0, which flips left and right. So:

> When you multiply or divide both sides of an inequality by a negative number, reverse the inequality symbol.

### Example 1

Solve $7 - 3x \ge 19$ and graph the solution.

1. Subtract 7 from both sides: $-3x \ge 12$.
2. Divide by $-3$ and reverse the symbol: $x \le -4$.
3. Check a value from the answer, say $x = -5$: $7 - 3(-5) = 22 \ge 19$. True. Check one outside, $x = 0$: $7 \ge 19$ is false, as it should be.

```numberline
{"x": [-9, 3], "points": [{"at": [-4, 0], "label": "-4"}], "segments": [{"from": [-4, 0], "to": [-9, 0], "arrow": true}], "caption": "x ≤ -4: closed dot at -4, shading to the left"}
```

The dot at $-4$ is solid (closed) because $-4$ itself is a solution. For a strict inequality like $<$ or $>$, the endpoint is not included and the dot is drawn open.

You can avoid dividing by a negative by moving the variable term to the other side instead: $7 - 19 \ge 3x$, so $-12 \ge 3x$, or $-4 \ge x$. That says the same thing as $x \le -4$, read from the other side.

## Interval notation

**[[Interval notation]]** writes a set of numbers by its endpoints. A square bracket means the endpoint is included; a parenthesis means it is not. Infinity is never a number you reach, so $\infty$ and $-\infty$ always get parentheses.

| Inequality | Interval | Number line |
|---|---|---|
| $x > 2$ | $(2, \infty)$ | open dot at 2, shade right |
| $x \le -4$ | $(-\infty, -4]$ | closed dot at $-4$, shade left |
| $-1 < x \le 3$ | $(-1, 3]$ | open at $-1$, closed at 3 |
| all real numbers | $(-\infty, \infty)$ | whole line |

The **[[set-builder notation]]** $\{x \mid x > 2\}$, read "the set of all $x$ such that $x > 2$," is another common way to write the same set.

### Example 2

Solve $\dfrac{x}{2} + 1 < \dfrac{2x - 1}{3}$. Write the answer in interval notation.

1. Multiply every term by 6 (positive, so no flip): $3x + 6 < 2(2x - 1)$.
2. Distribute: $3x + 6 < 4x - 2$.
3. Subtract $3x$ and add 2: $8 < x$.
4. So $x > 8$, which is $(8, \infty)$.
5. Check $x = 11$: $5.5 + 1 = 6.5$ and $\tfrac{21}{3} = 7$, and $6.5 < 7$. True.

## Compound inequalities with "and"

A **[[compound inequality]]** joins two inequalities. With "and," a number must satisfy both, so the solution is the **[[intersection]]** of the two solution sets: the overlap. "$x > -2$ and $x \le 3$" is usually written as the **[[double inequality]]** $-2 < x \le 3$.

To solve a double inequality, do the same operation to all three parts at once.

### Example 3

Solve $-5 \le 2x + 3 < 9$.

1. Subtract 3 from all three parts: $-8 \le 2x < 6$.
2. Divide all three parts by 2: $-4 \le x < 3$.
3. Interval: $[-4, 3)$.

```numberline
{"x": [-7, 6], "points": [{"at": [-4, 0], "label": "-4"}, {"at": [3, 0], "open": true, "label": "3"}], "segments": [{"from": [-4, 0], "to": [3, 0]}], "caption": "-4 ≤ x < 3, the interval [-4, 3)"}
```

If you divide all three parts by a negative number, both symbols flip. For $1 < 5 - 2x < 11$: subtract 5 to get $-4 < -2x < 6$, divide by $-2$ to get $2 > x > -3$, and rewrite in increasing order as $-3 < x < 2$.

## Compound inequalities with "or"

With "or," a number needs to satisfy at least one of the inequalities, so the solution is the **[[union]]** of the two sets, written with $\cup$. Solve each part separately, then combine.

### Example 4

Solve $3x - 1 < -7$ or $2x + 5 \ge 11$.

1. First part: $3x < -6$, so $x < -2$.
2. Second part: $2x \ge 6$, so $x \ge 3$.
3. Union: $x < -2$ or $x \ge 3$, which is $(-\infty, -2) \cup [3, \infty)$.

```numberline
{"x": [-7, 7], "points": [{"at": [-2, 0], "open": true, "label": "-2"}, {"at": [3, 0], "label": "3"}], "segments": [{"from": [-2, 0], "to": [-7, 0], "arrow": true}, {"from": [3, 0], "to": [7, 0], "arrow": true}], "caption": "x < -2 or x ≥ 3: two separate rays"}
```

Watch for special cases. "$x > 4$ and $x < 1$" has no overlap, so it has no solution. "$x > 1$ or $x < 4$" covers every real number, because each number is either above 1 or below 4 (or both).

## Inequalities in applications

Words like "at least" ($\ge$), "at most" ($\le$), "more than" ($>$), "less than" ($<$), "no more than" ($\le$) and "minimum" or "maximum" signal an inequality.

### Example 5

A phone plan costs $25 a month plus $0.10 per text. How many texts can you send if you want the bill to be at most $40?

1. Let $t$ be the number of texts: $25 + 0.10t \le 40$.
2. Subtract 25: $0.10t \le 15$. Divide by 0.10: $t \le 150$.
3. You can send at most 150 texts. (Since $t$ counts texts, the realistic answers are the whole numbers from 0 to 150.)

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting to flip the symbol when multiplying or dividing by a negative. Moving a term across with addition never flips anything.
- Flipping the symbol when the coefficient is negative but you divided by a positive number.
- Using a bracket next to $\infty$. Infinity always takes a parenthesis.
- Writing an "or" answer as a double inequality: $x < -2$ or $x \ge 3$ is not $3 \le x < -2$, which describes no numbers at all.
- Confusing intersection (and, overlap) with union (or, everything in either).

## Key points

- Solve linear inequalities like equations, but reverse the symbol when multiplying or dividing by a negative.
- Closed dot or bracket: endpoint included ($\le$, $\ge$). Open dot or parenthesis: not included ($<$, $>$), and always next to $\pm\infty$.
- "And" means intersection; solve a double inequality by operating on all three parts.
- "Or" means union; solve each part and combine with $\cup$.

lessons.title: Absolute value equations and inequalities
lessons.body:
In Lesson 1 we defined $|a|$ as the distance from $a$ to 0. That one idea turns absolute value equations and inequalities into problems you already know how to solve: a pair of linear equations, a double inequality, or an "or" inequality. This lesson shows how to make the translation and why it works.

## Absolute value as distance

Because $|x|$ is the distance from $x$ to 0:

- $|x| = 4$ means $x$ is 4 units from 0, so $x = 4$ or $x = -4$.
- $|x| < 4$ means $x$ is less than 4 units from 0, so $-4 < x < 4$.
- $|x| > 4$ means $x$ is more than 4 units from 0, so $x < -4$ or $x > 4$.

```numberline
{"x": [-7, 7], "points": [{"at": [-4, 0], "open": true, "label": "-4"}, {"at": [4, 0], "open": true, "label": "4"}, {"at": [0, 0], "label": "0"}], "segments": [{"from": [-4, 0], "to": [4, 0]}], "caption": "|x| < 4: everything within 4 units of 0"}
```

More generally, $|x - c|$ is the distance from $x$ to $c$, so $|x - 3| < 2$ describes the numbers within 2 units of 3: the interval $(1, 5)$.

## Absolute value equations

For $k > 0$, the equation $|u| = k$ is equivalent to

$$u = k \quad \text{or} \quad u = -k,$$

where $u$ can be any expression. If $k = 0$, there is one solution: $u = 0$. If $k < 0$, there are no solutions, because a distance can't be negative.

Before splitting, isolate the absolute value: get $|u|$ alone on one side.

### Example 1

Solve $3|2x - 1| + 4 = 25$.

1. Isolate: subtract 4 to get $3|2x - 1| = 21$, then divide by 3 to get $|2x - 1| = 7$.
2. Split: $2x - 1 = 7$ or $2x - 1 = -7$.
3. Solve each: $2x = 8$ gives $x = 4$; $2x = -6$ gives $x = -3$.
4. Check: $3|7| + 4 = 25$ and $3|-7| + 4 = 25$. Both work.

A common slip is to split first, writing $3(2x - 1) + 4 = 25$ and $3(2x - 1) + 4 = -25$. The second is wrong: the negative belongs to what's inside the bars, not to the whole side.

### Example 2

Solve $|x + 5| + 8 = 3$.

Isolating gives $|x + 5| = -5$. An absolute value is never negative, so there is no solution. Spotting this saves you from producing two fake answers.

### Equations with two absolute values

If $|u| = |v|$, then $u$ and $v$ are the same distance from 0, so $u = v$ or $u = -v$. For $|x - 2| = |3x + 4|$: either $x - 2 = 3x + 4$, giving $x = -3$, or $x - 2 = -(3x + 4)$, giving $4x = -2$ and $x = -\tfrac12$. Check: $|-5| = |-5|$ and $|-\tfrac52| = |\tfrac52|$.

## "Less than" inequalities become "and"

For $k > 0$:

$$|u| < k \iff -k < u < k, \qquad |u| \le k \iff -k \le u \le k.$$

The values of $u$ are trapped between $-k$ and $k$, so the solution is a single interval. Think "less than → between."

### Example 3

Solve $|2x - 3| \le 5$.

1. Rewrite as a double inequality: $-5 \le 2x - 3 \le 5$.
2. Add 3 to all parts: $-2 \le 2x \le 8$.
3. Divide by 2: $-1 \le x \le 4$, the interval $[-1, 4]$.

The midpoint of $[-1, 4]$ is $1.5 = \tfrac32$, which is where $2x - 3 = 0$, and the interval reaches $\tfrac52$ on each side. That matches the distance picture: $|2x - 3| \le 5$ is the same as $|x - \tfrac32| \le \tfrac52$.

## "Greater than" inequalities become "or"

For $k > 0$:

$$|u| > k \iff u < -k \text{ or } u > k.$$

The values of $u$ are far from 0 in either direction, so the solution is two separate rays. Think "greater than → or."

### Example 4

Solve $|x + 1| - 2 > 4$.

1. Isolate: $|x + 1| > 6$.
2. Split: $x + 1 < -6$ or $x + 1 > 6$.
3. Solve: $x < -7$ or $x > 5$, which is $(-\infty, -7) \cup (5, \infty)$.

```numberline
{"x": [-11, 9], "points": [{"at": [-7, 0], "open": true, "label": "-7"}, {"at": [5, 0], "open": true, "label": "5"}, {"at": [-1, 0], "label": "-1"}], "segments": [{"from": [-7, 0], "to": [-11, 0], "arrow": true}, {"from": [5, 0], "to": [9, 0], "arrow": true}], "caption": "|x + 1| > 6: more than 6 units from -1"}
```

## Special cases with negative or zero right sides

Once the absolute value is isolated, look at the number on the other side before splitting.

| Inequality | Solution | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| $\lvert u \rvert < -3$ | none | a distance is never below a negative number |
| $\lvert u \rvert > -3$ | all real numbers (where $u$ is defined) | every distance is at least 0 |
| $\lvert u \rvert \le 0$ | only where $u = 0$ | the distance must be exactly 0 |
| $\lvert u \rvert > 0$ | everything except where $u = 0$ | every nonzero distance is positive |

## A graphical view

You can also read absolute value inequalities from a graph. The graph of $y = |x - 2|$ is a V with its corner at $(2, 0)$. The solutions of $|x - 2| < 3$ are the $x$-values where the V lies below the horizontal line $y = 3$.

```plot
{"x": [-3, 7], "y": [-1, 6], "functions": [{"f": "abs(x - 2)", "label": "y = |x - 2|"}, {"f": "3", "label": "y = 3", "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [-1, 3], "label": "(-1, 3)"}, {"at": [5, 3], "label": "(5, 3)"}], "caption": "The V is below y = 3 for -1 < x < 5"}
```

The V is below the line between $x = -1$ and $x = 5$, so $|x - 2| < 3$ has solution $(-1, 5)$, and $|x - 2| > 3$ has solution $(-\infty, -1) \cup (5, \infty)$.

## Common mistakes

- Splitting before isolating the absolute value.
- Writing $|u| = k$ as $u = k$ only, losing the negative case.
- Using "and" for a greater-than inequality: $|x| > 4$ is not $-4 > x > 4$, which no number satisfies.
- Missing the special cases: $|u| = -2$ and $|u| < -2$ have no solutions.
- Forgetting to flip the inequality when a negative coefficient shows up while solving the pieces.

## Key points

- $|u| = k$ with $k > 0$ splits into $u = k$ or $u = -k$; with $k < 0$ there's no solution.
- Isolate the absolute value first.
- $|u| < k$ becomes $-k < u < k$ (between, one interval).
- $|u| > k$ becomes $u < -k$ or $u > k$ (two rays).
- $|x - c|$ is the distance from $x$ to $c$, which explains all of the rules.

lessons.title: Functions and function notation
lessons.body:
So far each problem has asked for one unknown number. Much of algebra, and nearly all of science, is instead about how one quantity depends on another: distance on time, cost on quantity, temperature on altitude. The tool for describing that dependence is the function. This lesson defines functions, introduces the notation $f(x)$, and shows how to evaluate and interpret it.

## Relations and functions

A **[[relation]]** is any set of ordered pairs $(x, y)$. The first coordinates form its **[[domain]]** (the inputs) and the second coordinates form its **[[range]]** (the outputs).

A **[[function]]** is a relation in which each input has exactly one output. The input may be called the **[[independent variable]]** and the output the **[[dependent variable]]**, because the output depends on which input you choose.

- $\{(1, 4), (2, 7), (3, 4)\}$ is a function. Two inputs share the output 4, which is allowed.
- $\{(1, 4), (1, 6), (2, 7)\}$ is not a function, because the input 1 has two outputs.

The test is about inputs, not outputs: a function may repeat outputs but never assigns two outputs to one input. Think of a vending machine: each button gives one item. Two buttons giving the same snack is fine; one button giving either of two snacks at random is not a function.

## Functions described different ways

A function can be given as a table, a set of pairs, a rule in words, an equation, or a graph.

| $x$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ | $3$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-3$ | $-5$ |

The table above follows the rule "double $x$, subtract from 1," the equation $y = 1 - 2x$. Each description has its uses: tables are concrete, equations let you compute any value, and graphs show the overall shape at a glance.

An equation in $x$ and $y$ defines $y$ as a function of $x$ if each $x$ gives only one $y$. The equation $y = x^2$ does: each $x$ has one square. The equation $y^2 = x$ does not: for $x = 4$, both $y = 2$ and $y = -2$ work.

## The vertical line test

On a graph, an input $x = a$ corresponds to the vertical line through $a$. If some vertical line crosses the graph twice, that input has two outputs. So:

> **[[Vertical line test]]**: a graph represents a function exactly when no vertical line crosses it more than once.

```plot
{"x": [-1, 9], "y": [-4, 4], "functions": [{"f": "sqrt(x)", "label": "y = √x"}, {"f": "-sqrt(x)", "label": "y = -√x", "dashed": true}], "segments": [{"from": [4, -4], "to": [4, 4], "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [4, 2], "label": "(4, 2)"}, {"at": [4, -2], "label": "(4, -2)"}], "caption": "The whole curve y² = x fails the vertical line test at x = 4; its top half alone is a function"}
```

## Function notation

If a function is named $f$, then $f(x)$, read "$f$ of $x$," means the output of $f$ for the input $x$. It does not mean $f$ times $x$. Writing $f(x) = 1 - 2x$ is just a way to name the rule $y = 1 - 2x$ so we can talk about specific inputs: $f(3) = 1 - 2(3) = -5$ says that the point $(3, -5)$ is on the graph.

Function notation is compact and precise. "The value of $y$ when $x$ is 3" becomes $f(3)$, and if several functions are around we can name them $f$, $g$, $h$ or something meaningful like $C(n)$ for the cost of $n$ items.

### Example 1

Let $f(x) = 2x^2 - 3x + 1$. Find $f(-2)$, $f(0)$ and $f(a + 1)$.

1. $f(-2) = 2(-2)^2 - 3(-2) + 1 = 8 + 6 + 1 = 15$.
2. $f(0) = 0 - 0 + 1 = 1$.
3. Replace every $x$ by $(a + 1)$, keeping the parentheses:
$$f(a + 1) = 2(a + 1)^2 - 3(a + 1) + 1 = 2(a^2 + 2a + 1) - 3a - 3 + 1 = 2a^2 + a.$$

The input can be any expression. Whatever goes in the parentheses replaces $x$ everywhere.

### Example 2

Let $g(x) = 5 - 3x$. Solve $g(x) = 17$.

This asks a different question: which input gives the output 17? Set up the equation $5 - 3x = 17$, so $-3x = 12$ and $x = -4$. Check: $g(-4) = 5 + 12 = 17$.

Keep the two kinds of question apart. $g(17)$ asks for an output (it equals $5 - 51 = -46$); $g(x) = 17$ asks for an input.

## Reading values from a graph

On the graph of $f$, the point above (or below) $x = a$ has height $f(a)$. So $f(a)$ is read by going to $a$ on the $x$-axis and moving vertically to the curve. To solve $f(x) = c$, go to height $c$ on the $y$-axis and move horizontally to find where the curve is at that height.

```plot
{"x": [-3, 5], "y": [-5, 6], "functions": [{"f": "x^2 - 2*x - 3", "label": "y = f(x)"}], "points": [{"at": [3, 0], "label": "(3, 0)"}, {"at": [-1, 0], "label": "(-1, 0)"}, {"at": [0, -3], "label": "(0, -3)"}, {"at": [4, 5], "label": "(4, 5)"}], "caption": "f(0) = -3, f(4) = 5, and f(x) = 0 at x = -1 and x = 3"}
```

From this graph: $f(0) = -3$ (the curve crosses the $y$-axis at $-3$) and $f(4) = 5$. The equation $f(x) = 0$ has two solutions, $x = -1$ and $x = 3$, where the curve meets the $x$-axis.

## Functions in context

### Example 3

A streaming service charges a $12 monthly fee plus $4 per rental. Write the cost as a function of the number of rentals $r$, find $C(5)$, and interpret it.

1. $C(r) = 12 + 4r$.
2. $C(5) = 12 + 4(5) = 32$.
3. Interpretation: renting 5 movies in a month costs $32.

Here $r$ is the independent variable and $C$ is the dependent variable. A sensible domain is the whole numbers $0, 1, 2, \dots$, since you can't rent half a movie. That idea, the domain allowed by the situation, is the subject of the next lesson.

## Combining functions

Functions can be added, subtracted, multiplied and divided output by output: $(f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)$, and so on. You can also feed the output of one function into another. The **[[composition]]** $f(g(x))$ means "apply $g$, then apply $f$ to the result." If $f(x) = x^2$ and $g(x) = x + 3$, then $f(g(2)) = f(5) = 25$, while $g(f(2)) = g(4) = 7$. Order matters.

## Common mistakes

- Reading $f(x)$ as multiplication.
- Substituting an expression without parentheses: $f(a + 1)$ for $f(x) = x^2$ is $(a + 1)^2$, not $a + 1^2$.
- Confusing $f(3)$ (an output) with solving $f(x) = 3$ (finding inputs).
- Thinking a repeated output breaks the function rule. Only repeated inputs with different outputs do.
- Mixing up the order in a composition: $f(g(x))$ applies $g$ first.

## Key points

- A function assigns exactly one output to each input; the inputs form the domain and the outputs form the range.
- The vertical line test checks whether a graph is a function.
- $f(a)$ is the output for input $a$, and the point $(a, f(a))$ lies on the graph.
- To evaluate, replace every $x$ with the input in parentheses; to solve $f(x) = c$, set up an equation.
- $f(g(x))$ means apply $g$ first, then $f$.

lessons.title: Domain, range, and graphs of functions
lessons.body:
The last lesson defined a function's domain and range as its sets of inputs and outputs. This lesson shows how to find them: from a formula, from a graph, and from a real situation. It also builds the habit of reading a graph for its key features, such as intercepts, where it rises and falls, and its highest and lowest points.

## Domain from a formula

When a function is given only by a formula, its domain is every real number for which the formula makes sense. In algebra, two things can go wrong:

1. *Division by zero.* A denominator can't be 0.
2. *Even roots of negative numbers.* $\sqrt{u}$ (and $\sqrt[4]{u}$, and so on) requires $u \ge 0$ to give a real number.

Polynomials like $3x^2 - x + 5$ have neither problem, so their domain is all real numbers, $(-\infty, \infty)$. Odd roots, like $\sqrt[3]{x}$, work for negative inputs too.

### Example 1

Find the domain of $f(x) = \dfrac{x + 2}{x - 5}$ and of $g(x) = \sqrt{3 - 2x}$.

1. For $f$, the only problem is a zero denominator: $x - 5 = 0$ at $x = 5$. Domain: all reals except 5, written $(-\infty, 5) \cup (5, \infty)$.
2. For $g$, the radicand must be nonnegative: $3 - 2x \ge 0$, so $-2x \ge -3$ and (dividing by $-2$, flipping) $x \le \tfrac32$. Domain: $(-\infty, \tfrac32]$.

### Example 2

Find the domain of $h(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x + 4}}$.

The square root needs $x + 4 \ge 0$, and it's in the denominator so it also can't be 0. Together, $x + 4 > 0$, so $x > -4$. Domain: $(-4, \infty)$.

## Domain and range from a graph

On a graph, the domain is the set of $x$-values the graph covers, which you see by squashing the graph flat onto the $x$-axis. The range is the set of $y$-values it covers, seen by squashing it onto the $y$-axis. Solid dots mean an endpoint is included, open dots mean it isn't, and arrows mean the graph continues forever.

```plot
{"x": [-4, 6], "y": [-6, 5], "functions": [{"f": "-(x - 1)^2 + 4", "from": -2, "to": 4}], "points": [{"at": [-2, -5], "label": "(-2, -5)"}, {"at": [4, -5], "open": true, "label": "(4, -5)"}, {"at": [1, 4], "label": "(1, 4)"}, {"at": [-1, 0], "label": "(-1, 0)"}, {"at": [3, 0], "label": "(3, 0)"}, {"at": [0, 3], "label": "(0, 3)"}], "caption": "A parabola segment from x = -2 (closed dot) to x = 4 (open dot)"}
```

The graph above is $f(x) = -(x - 1)^2 + 4$ restricted to $-2 \le x < 4$, with a closed dot at the left end and an open dot at the right end. Both ends are at height $-5$.

- Domain: the $x$-values run from $-2$ (included) to 4 (not included): $[-2, 4)$.
- Range: the highest point is the vertex at height 4. The lowest height reached is $-5$, at the included left endpoint. So the range is $[-5, 4]$. Note that the open dot at the right doesn't matter for the range, because the height $-5$ is already reached at $x = -2$.

## Key features of a graph

Reading a graph means answering a handful of standard questions.

- *Intercepts.* The **[[y-intercept]]** is where the graph crosses the $y$-axis, the point $(0, f(0))$. An **[[x-intercept]]** is where it meets the $x$-axis; those $x$-values are the **[[zeros]]** of $f$, the solutions of $f(x) = 0$. Above, the $y$-intercept is $(0, 3)$ and the zeros are $-1$ and 3.
- *Increasing and decreasing.* A function is **[[increasing]]** on an interval if the graph rises as you move right, and **[[decreasing]]** if it falls. Above, $f$ increases on $(-2, 1)$ and decreases on $(1, 4)$. These intervals describe $x$-values.
- *Maximum and minimum.* The highest point gives the **[[maximum value]]** (here 4, at $x = 1$). The lowest gives the **[[minimum value]]**.
- *Sign.* $f(x) > 0$ where the graph is above the $x$-axis (here on $(-1, 3)$), and $f(x) < 0$ where it is below.

### Example 3

The graph shows $g(x) = |x + 1| - 2$.

```plot
{"x": [-6, 4], "y": [-3, 4], "functions": [{"f": "abs(x + 1) - 2", "label": "y = g(x)"}], "points": [{"at": [-1, -2], "label": "(-1, -2)"}, {"at": [-3, 0], "label": "(-3, 0)"}, {"at": [1, 0], "label": "(1, 0)"}, {"at": [0, -1], "label": "(0, -1)"}], "caption": "g(x) = |x + 1| - 2"}
```

1. Domain: the V extends forever both ways, so $(-\infty, \infty)$.
2. Range: the lowest point is the corner at height $-2$, and the arms go up forever: $[-2, \infty)$.
3. Zeros: $x = -3$ and $x = 1$. Check: $g(1) = |2| - 2 = 0$.
4. $y$-intercept: $g(0) = 1 - 2 = -1$.
5. Decreasing on $(-\infty, -1)$, increasing on $(-1, \infty)$, minimum value $-2$.
6. $g(x) < 0$ for $-3 < x < 1$, where the V dips below the axis.

## Domain from context

A formula may make sense for more inputs than the situation allows. If a ball's height after $t$ seconds is $h(t) = -16t^2 + 64t$, the formula works for any $t$, but the physical model only applies from launch ($t = 0$) until it lands. The height is 0 at launch ($t = 0$) and again at $t = 4$, since $h(4) = -16(16) + 64(4) = -256 + 256 = 0$, so the practical domain is $[0, 4]$. The **[[practical domain]]** (or reasonable domain) is the set of inputs that make sense in context.

## A gallery of basic functions

These shapes appear again and again; knowing their domains and ranges by sight saves work.

| Function | Domain | Range |
|---|---|---|
| $f(x) = x$ | $(-\infty, \infty)$ | $(-\infty, \infty)$ |
| $f(x) = x^2$ | $(-\infty, \infty)$ | $[0, \infty)$ |
| $f(x) = \lvert x \rvert$ | $(-\infty, \infty)$ | $[0, \infty)$ |
| $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ | $[0, \infty)$ | $[0, \infty)$ |
| $f(x) = \tfrac{1}{x}$ | $x \ne 0$ | $y \ne 0$ |
| $f(x) = x^3$ | $(-\infty, \infty)$ | $(-\infty, \infty)$ |

```plot
{"x": [-4, 4], "y": [-3, 5], "functions": [{"f": "x^2", "label": "x²"}, {"f": "sqrt(x)", "label": "√x", "dashed": true}, {"f": "x^3", "label": "x³", "from": -2.4, "to": 2.4}], "caption": "Three basic shapes: the parabola x², the half-parabola √x and the cubic x³"}
```

## Common mistakes

- Giving the domain as $y$-values or the range as $x$-values. Domain is horizontal, range is vertical.
- Forgetting to exclude values that make a denominator zero, or including them when the root is in a denominator.
- Writing increasing/decreasing intervals with $y$-values instead of $x$-values.
- Treating an open endpoint as excluding a range value that is reached elsewhere on the graph.
- Ignoring the context: negative times or lengths are usually not in the practical domain.

## Key points

- Domain from a formula: exclude zeros of denominators and inputs that make even roots negative.
- On a graph, the domain is the horizontal extent and the range is the vertical extent.
- Zeros are the $x$-intercepts; the $y$-intercept is $(0, f(0))$.
- Increasing and decreasing intervals, and positive and negative intervals, are stated in terms of $x$.
- In applications, restrict the domain to inputs that make sense.

lessons.title: Slope and rate of change
lessons.body:
The simplest functions are the ones whose graphs are straight lines. What makes a line straight is that it rises or falls at a constant rate, and the number that measures that rate is the slope. This lesson defines slope, shows how to compute it from points, a graph or a table, and explains what it means in real situations. The next lesson uses slope to write equations of lines.

## Rise over run

Pick two points on a line. Moving from the first to the second, the vertical change is the **[[rise]]** and the horizontal change is the **[[run]]**. The **[[slope]]** $m$ is their ratio:

$$m = \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}.$$

The Greek letter delta is often used for "change in," so you'll also see $m = \dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$.

```plot
{"x": [-1, 7], "y": [-1, 7], "functions": [{"f": "0.75*x + 1", "label": "y = 0.75x + 1"}], "points": [{"at": [0, 1], "label": "(0, 1)"}, {"at": [4, 4], "label": "(4, 4)"}], "segments": [{"from": [0, 1], "to": [4, 1], "dashed": true, "label": "run 4"}, {"from": [4, 1], "to": [4, 4], "dashed": true, "label": "rise 3"}], "equal": true, "caption": "From (0, 1) to (4, 4): rise 3, run 4, slope 3/4"}
```

Why is the slope the same no matter which two points you choose? Any two "slope triangles" on the same line are similar triangles: they have the same angles, so the ratio of their vertical side to their horizontal side is the same. That constant ratio is exactly what makes the graph a straight line.

### Example 1

Find the slope of the line through $(-2, 5)$ and $(4, -7)$.

1. Label: $(x_1, y_1) = (-2, 5)$ and $(x_2, y_2) = (4, -7)$.
2. $m = \dfrac{-7 - 5}{4 - (-2)} = \dfrac{-12}{6} = -2$.
3. Swapping the points gives $\dfrac{5 - (-7)}{-2 - 4} = \dfrac{12}{-6} = -2$, the same. Just be consistent: subtract in the same order on top and bottom.

## What the sign of the slope tells you

| Slope | Line | Example |
|---|---|---|
| $m > 0$ | rises from left to right | $y = 2x$ |
| $m < 0$ | falls from left to right | $y = -x + 3$ |
| $m = 0$ | horizontal | $y = 4$ |
| undefined | vertical | $x = -1$ |

A **[[horizontal line]]** has rise 0 for every run, so its slope is $0$. A **[[vertical line]]** has run 0, and dividing by zero is undefined, so a vertical line has **[[undefined slope]]**. Don't confuse "zero slope" with "no slope": they describe opposite lines.

The size of the slope measures steepness. A line with slope $-5$ is steeper than one with slope $2$, because $|-5| > |2|$.

```plot
{"x": [-4, 4], "y": [-4, 4], "functions": [{"f": "3*x", "label": "m = 3"}, {"f": "0.5*x", "label": "m = 1/2"}, {"f": "-x", "label": "m = -1", "dashed": true}, {"f": "-2", "label": "m = 0"}], "equal": true, "caption": "Larger |m| means steeper; the sign gives the direction"}
```

### Example 2

Find the slope through $(3, -1)$ and $(3, 6)$, and through $(-4, 2)$ and $(5, 2)$.

1. First pair: $m = \dfrac{6 - (-1)}{3 - 3} = \dfrac{7}{0}$, undefined. Both points have $x = 3$, so the line is vertical: $x = 3$.
2. Second pair: $m = \dfrac{2 - 2}{5 - (-4)} = \dfrac{0}{9} = 0$. The line is horizontal: $y = 2$.

## Slope from a graph

To read slope from a graph, find two points where the line crosses grid intersections exactly, then count the rise (up is positive, down is negative) and the run (right is positive). Choosing points far apart reduces the effect of small reading errors.

## Slope from a table

In a table of a linear function, the outputs change by the same amount for each equal step in the inputs.

| $x$ | 1 | 3 | 5 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ | 10 | 16 | 22 | 28 |

Each step of 2 in $x$ adds 6 to $y$, so the slope is $\tfrac{6}{2} = 3$. If the changes in $y$ were not proportional to the changes in $x$, the data would not lie on a line.

## Slope as a rate of change

Slope carries units: units of the output per unit of the input. That makes it a **[[rate of change]]**.

### Example 3

A car's fuel tank holds 14 gallons after 60 miles and 9.5 gallons after 150 miles. Find and interpret the slope.

1. Points $(60, 14)$ and $(150, 9.5)$, with $x$ in miles and $y$ in gallons.
2. $m = \dfrac{9.5 - 14}{150 - 60} = \dfrac{-4.5}{90} = -0.05$ gallons per mile.
3. Interpretation: the tank loses 0.05 gallons for every mile driven (equivalently, the car gets $1 / 0.05 = 20$ miles per gallon). The negative sign says the amount of fuel is decreasing.

### Example 4

A hiking trail climbs from an elevation of 1,250 m to 1,610 m over a horizontal distance of 4.5 km. What is its average slope in meters per kilometer, and as a percent grade?

1. Rise: $1610 - 1250 = 360$ m. Run: $4.5$ km $= 4500$ m.
2. In meters per kilometer: $\dfrac{360}{4.5} = 80$ m/km.
3. As a pure ratio (same units): $\dfrac{360}{4500} = 0.08$, an 8% grade.

For a nonlinear graph, the slope between two points is called the **[[average rate of change]]** over that interval. It's the slope of the straight segment joining the two points.

## Common mistakes

- Subtracting in opposite orders on top and bottom, which flips the sign.
- Putting run over rise: slope is $\dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$, vertical over horizontal.
- Calling a vertical line's slope 0. Horizontal is 0; vertical is undefined.
- Forgetting units in an application, or mixing units (meters over kilometers) without saying so.
- Reading points off a graph that don't sit exactly on grid intersections.

## Key points

- $m = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$; any two points on a line give the same slope.
- Positive slope rises, negative falls, zero is horizontal, undefined is vertical.
- $|m|$ measures steepness.
- In context, slope is a rate of change with units "output per input."
- On a curve, the slope between two points is the average rate of change.

lessons.title: Equations of lines
lessons.body:
A line is determined by its slope and one point on it, or by any two of its points. This lesson turns that geometric fact into equations. You'll learn the three standard forms of a line's equation (slope-intercept, point-slope and standard form), when each is most convenient, and how to graph a line quickly from each.

## Slope-intercept form

A **[[linear function]]** has the form $f(x) = mx + b$. Its graph is a line with slope $m$ that crosses the $y$-axis at $(0, b)$. Writing the line as

$$y = mx + b$$

is called **[[slope-intercept form]]**. Why does it work? At $x = 0$, $y = b$, so $(0, b)$ is on the line. And each time $x$ increases by 1, $mx$ increases by $m$, so $y$ rises by $m$: that's a slope of $m$.

To graph $y = mx + b$: plot the $y$-intercept $(0, b)$, then use the slope as rise over run to step to a second point, and draw the line through them.

### Example 1

Graph $y = -\tfrac{2}{3}x + 4$.

1. The $y$-intercept is $(0, 4)$.
2. The slope $-\tfrac23$ means down 2 for every 3 to the right. From $(0, 4)$ step to $(3, 2)$, then to $(6, 0)$.
3. Draw the line. It crosses the $x$-axis at $(6, 0)$.

```plot
{"x": [-3, 8], "y": [-2, 7], "functions": [{"f": "-2/3*x + 4", "label": "y = -2/3 x + 4"}], "points": [{"at": [0, 4], "label": "(0, 4)"}, {"at": [3, 2], "label": "(3, 2)"}, {"at": [6, 0], "label": "(6, 0)"}], "segments": [{"from": [0, 4], "to": [3, 4], "dashed": true, "label": "run 3"}, {"from": [3, 4], "to": [3, 2], "dashed": true, "label": "rise -2"}], "equal": true, "caption": "Start at the y-intercept, then step with the slope"}
```

## Point-slope form

If you know the slope $m$ and any point $(x_1, y_1)$ on the line, then for any other point $(x, y)$ on it, the slope formula says $\dfrac{y - y_1}{x - x_1} = m$. Multiply both sides by $x - x_1$:

$$y - y_1 = m(x - x_1).$$

This is **[[point-slope form]]**. It's the most direct way to write a line's equation when you aren't given the $y$-intercept.

### Example 2

Write an equation of the line through $(2, -3)$ with slope 4, in slope-intercept form.

1. Point-slope: $y - (-3) = 4(x - 2)$, that is $y + 3 = 4(x - 2)$.
2. Distribute: $y + 3 = 4x - 8$.
3. Subtract 3: $y = 4x - 11$.
4. Check: at $x = 2$, $y = 8 - 11 = -3$. Correct.

### Example 3

Write an equation of the line through $(-1, 6)$ and $(3, -2)$.

1. Slope first: $m = \dfrac{-2 - 6}{3 - (-1)} = \dfrac{-8}{4} = -2$.
2. Point-slope with $(-1, 6)$: $y - 6 = -2(x + 1)$.
3. Simplify: $y - 6 = -2x - 2$, so $y = -2x + 4$.
4. Check the other point: $-2(3) + 4 = -2$. Correct.

Using the other point gives $y + 2 = -2(x - 3)$, which simplifies to the same $y = -2x + 4$.

## Standard form

The **[[standard form]]** of a line is

$$Ax + By = C,$$

usually with integers $A$, $B$, $C$ and $A \ge 0$. Every line can be written this way, including vertical lines ($x = 5$ is $1x + 0y = 5$), which slope-intercept form can't express.

Standard form makes the intercepts easy to find. Set $y = 0$ to get the $x$-intercept, and $x = 0$ to get the $y$-intercept.

### Example 4

Graph $3x - 4y = 12$ using its intercepts, and find its slope.

1. $x$-intercept: $3x = 12$, so $(4, 0)$.
2. $y$-intercept: $-4y = 12$, so $(0, -3)$.
3. Plot both and draw the line.
4. Slope: solve for $y$. $-4y = -3x + 12$, so $y = \tfrac34 x - 3$, and $m = \tfrac34$. In general, the slope of $Ax + By = C$ is $-\tfrac{A}{B}$.

```plot
{"x": [-3, 7], "y": [-5, 3], "functions": [{"f": "0.75*x - 3", "label": "3x - 4y = 12"}], "points": [{"at": [4, 0], "label": "(4, 0)"}, {"at": [0, -3], "label": "(0, -3)"}], "equal": true, "caption": "Intercepts make standard form quick to graph"}
```

## Horizontal and vertical lines

A horizontal line through $(a, b)$ has slope 0, so its equation is $y = b$: every point has the same $y$-coordinate. A vertical line through $(a, b)$ is $x = a$: every point has the same $x$-coordinate. A vertical line is not the graph of a function (it fails the vertical line test in the most dramatic way possible).

## Choosing a form

| You know | Start with | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| slope and $y$-intercept | $y = mx + b$ | fastest to graph |
| slope and a point | $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$ | then simplify if asked |
| two points | compute $m$, then point-slope | check with the second point |
| intercepts, or you need integer coefficients | $Ax + By = C$ | also handles vertical lines |

### Example 5

Write $y = \tfrac25 x - 3$ in standard form with integer coefficients.

1. Multiply by 5 to clear the fraction: $5y = 2x - 15$.
2. Move the $x$ term: $-2x + 5y = -15$.
3. Make $A$ positive by multiplying by $-1$: $2x - 5y = 15$.

## Common mistakes

- Sign errors in point-slope form: through $(-1, 6)$, it's $y - 6 = m(x + 1)$, because $x - (-1) = x + 1$.
- Reading the slope of $Ax + By = C$ as $A$. Solve for $y$ first; the slope is $-\tfrac{A}{B}$.
- Using the run as the rise when graphing from a slope.
- Writing the vertical line through $(4, 1)$ as $y = 4$. Vertical lines are $x = \ldots$
- Stopping at point-slope form when the problem asks for slope-intercept form.

## Key points

- Slope-intercept form $y = mx + b$: slope $m$, $y$-intercept $(0, b)$.
- Point-slope form $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$ comes straight from the slope formula.
- Standard form $Ax + By = C$: intercepts by setting $x$ or $y$ to 0; slope $-\tfrac{A}{B}$.
- Horizontal lines are $y = b$; vertical lines are $x = a$.
- From two points: find the slope, then use point-slope form.

lessons.title: Parallel and perpendicular lines; linear models
lessons.body:
Slope tells you the direction of a line, so comparing slopes tells you how two lines are positioned relative to each other. This lesson shows that parallel lines have equal slopes and perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals, then uses lines to model real data: writing a linear function from a description, interpreting its slope and intercept, and making predictions.

## Parallel lines

Two distinct lines in a plane are **[[parallel lines]]** if they never meet. Lines with the same slope rise at the same rate, so the gap between them never changes: they're parallel. Conversely, lines with different slopes must eventually cross. So:

> Two non-vertical lines are parallel exactly when they have the same slope and different $y$-intercepts. All vertical lines are parallel to each other.

If two lines have the same slope and the same intercept, they're the same line, not two parallel ones.

### Example 1

Write the equation of the line through $(4, -1)$ parallel to $3x + 2y = 6$.

1. Find the given line's slope: $2y = -3x + 6$, so $y = -\tfrac32 x + 3$ and $m = -\tfrac32$.
2. The new line has the same slope. Point-slope: $y + 1 = -\tfrac32(x - 4)$.
3. Simplify: $y + 1 = -\tfrac32 x + 6$, so $y = -\tfrac32 x + 5$.

## Perpendicular lines

**[[Perpendicular lines]]** meet at a right angle. Their slopes have a neat relationship: if one line has slope $m$ (not 0), a perpendicular line has slope $-\tfrac{1}{m}$, the **[[negative reciprocal]]**. Equivalently, the product of their slopes is $-1$.

Here's why. Take a slope triangle for the first line: run $a$, rise $b$, so $m = \tfrac{b}{a}$. Rotate the whole picture $90°$ counterclockwise. The run $a$ becomes a rise of $a$, and the rise $b$ becomes a run of $-b$ (pointing left). The rotated line is perpendicular to the original and has slope $\tfrac{a}{-b} = -\tfrac{a}{b} = -\tfrac{1}{m}$.

```plot
{"x": [-5, 5], "y": [-4, 4], "functions": [{"f": "2*x/3", "label": "m = 2/3"}, {"f": "-3*x/2", "label": "m = -3/2"}], "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [3, 0], "dashed": true}, {"from": [3, 0], "to": [3, 2], "dashed": true}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [0, 3], "dashed": true}, {"from": [0, 3], "to": [-2, 3], "dashed": true}], "rightAngles": [[[0, 0], [3, 2], [-2, 3]]], "equal": true, "caption": "Rotating the slope triangle 90° turns slope 2/3 into slope -3/2"}
```

Horizontal and vertical lines are perpendicular to each other; this is the case the formula can't handle, since 0 has no reciprocal.

| Line slope | Parallel slope | Perpendicular slope |
|---|---|---|
| $2$ | $2$ | $-\tfrac12$ |
| $-\tfrac34$ | $-\tfrac34$ | $\tfrac43$ |
| $0$ (horizontal) | $0$ | undefined (vertical) |

### Example 2

Write the equation of the line through $(-2, 5)$ perpendicular to $y = \tfrac25 x - 1$.

1. The given slope is $\tfrac25$. The perpendicular slope is $-\tfrac52$.
2. Point-slope: $y - 5 = -\tfrac52(x + 2)$.
3. Simplify: $y - 5 = -\tfrac52 x - 5$, so $y = -\tfrac52 x$.
4. Check: at $x = -2$, $y = 5$. And $\tfrac25 \cdot \left(-\tfrac52\right) = -1$.

### Example 3

Are the lines $4x - 6y = 3$ and $3x + 2y = 8$ parallel, perpendicular or neither?

1. Slopes: $-\tfrac{A}{B}$ gives $-\tfrac{4}{-6} = \tfrac23$ and $-\tfrac32$.
2. Product: $\tfrac23 \cdot \left(-\tfrac32\right) = -1$. The lines are perpendicular.

## Linear models

A **[[linear model]]** describes a quantity that changes at a constant rate. In $y = mx + b$ form:

- the slope $m$ is the rate of change (units of $y$ per unit of $x$);
- the intercept $b$ is the starting value, the output when the input is 0.

### Example 4

A plumber charges a fixed call-out fee plus an hourly rate. A 2-hour job costs $190 and a 5-hour job costs $385. Write the cost $C$ as a function of hours $h$, interpret the parameters, and predict the cost of a 3.5-hour job.

1. Two data points: $(2, 190)$ and $(5, 385)$.
2. Slope: $m = \dfrac{385 - 190}{5 - 2} = \dfrac{195}{3} = 65$ dollars per hour.
3. Point-slope: $C - 190 = 65(h - 2)$, so $C = 65h + 60$.
4. Interpretation: $65 an hour, plus a $60 call-out fee (the cost at $h = 0$).
5. Prediction: $C(3.5) = 65(3.5) + 60 = 287.50$ dollars.

```plot
{"x": [0, 7], "y": [0, 520], "functions": [{"f": "65*x + 60", "label": "C = 65h + 60"}], "points": [{"at": [2, 190], "label": "(2, 190)"}, {"at": [5, 385], "label": "(5, 385)"}, {"at": [3.5, 287.5], "label": "(3.5, 287.5)"}], "xLabel": "hours", "yLabel": "cost ($)", "caption": "A linear cost model"}
```

### Example 5

A city had 48,000 residents in 2010 and 55,200 in 2022. Assuming linear growth, write a model and estimate the population in 2030.

1. Let $t$ be years since 2010. Points $(0, 48000)$ and $(12, 55200)$.
2. Slope: $\dfrac{7200}{12} = 600$ people per year. Intercept: 48,000.
3. Model: $P(t) = 600t + 48000$.
4. 2030 is $t = 20$: $P(20) = 12000 + 48000 = 60000$.

Predicting inside the range of your data (**[[interpolation]]**) is usually safer than predicting beyond it (**[[extrapolation]]**), because the trend may not continue.

## Using slopes in geometry

Slopes give a quick test for right angles and parallel sides in figures on a coordinate grid.

### Example 6

Show that the triangle with vertices $O(0, 0)$, $A(4, 2)$ and $B(3, 4)$ is a right triangle.

1. Slope of $OA$: $\tfrac{2 - 0}{4 - 0} = \tfrac12$.
2. Slope of $AB$: $\tfrac{4 - 2}{3 - 4} = -2$.
3. The product is $\tfrac12 \cdot (-2) = -1$, so $OA \perp AB$ and the triangle has a right angle at $A$.

```plot
{"x": [-1, 6], "y": [-1, 5], "equal": true, "polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [4, 2], [3, 4]]}], "rightAngles": [[[4, 2], [0, 0], [3, 4]]], "points": [{"at": [0, 0], "label": "O"}, {"at": [4, 2], "label": "A"}, {"at": [3, 4], "label": "B"}], "caption": "Slopes 1/2 and -2 multiply to -1: a right angle at A"}
```

## Common mistakes

- Using the reciprocal without changing the sign (or the opposite without flipping) for a perpendicular slope. Both changes are needed.
- Calling lines with equal slopes parallel when they also have the same intercept: that's one line.
- Comparing slopes without first solving for $y$ (or using $-\tfrac{A}{B}$).
- Mixing up the slope and intercept in a model: the fixed fee is the intercept, the per-unit rate is the slope.
- Trusting extrapolations far outside the data.

## Key points

- Parallel: equal slopes (different intercepts). Perpendicular: slopes multiply to $-1$, $m_2 = -\tfrac{1}{m_1}$.
- Horizontal and vertical lines are perpendicular to each other.
- In a linear model, slope is the constant rate of change and the intercept is the starting value.
- Build a model from two data points just like a line through two points.
- Interpolation is more reliable than extrapolation.

lessons.title: Systems of equations by graphing and substitution
lessons.body:
Many problems involve two unknowns tied together by two conditions: two prices and two purchases, two speeds and two trips. Each condition is a linear equation, and the pair forms a system. This lesson explains what a solution of a system means, how to see it on a graph, and how to find it exactly with the substitution method.

## What a system is

A **[[system of linear equations]]** is a set of linear equations in the same variables, considered together. For example,

$$\begin{cases} x + y = 7 \\ 2x - y = 2 \end{cases}$$

A **[[solution of a system]]** is an ordered pair $(x, y)$ that makes every equation true at the same time. $(3, 4)$ satisfies the first equation ($3 + 4 = 7$) and the second ($2(3) - 4 = 2$), so it is a solution. $(5, 2)$ satisfies the first ($5 + 2 = 7$) but not the second ($10 - 2 = 8$), so it is not.

## Solving by graphing

Each equation's solutions form a line. A point that lies on both lines satisfies both equations. So the solutions of the system are the intersection points of the lines.

```plot
{"x": [-2, 8], "y": [-3, 9], "functions": [{"f": "7 - x", "label": "x + y = 7"}, {"f": "2*x - 2", "label": "2x - y = 2"}], "points": [{"at": [3, 4], "label": "(3, 4)"}], "caption": "The lines cross at (3, 4), the solution of the system"}
```

Two lines in a plane can relate in only three ways, so a linear system has exactly one solution, none, or infinitely many.

| Lines | Number of solutions | Name |
|---|---|---|
